notes: signals 1,2,4 — iterative ownership chasing, working file kept, corpus exceeds a prompt
workload: Onboarding a new supplier means establishing who ultimately owns it, and the answer is rarely one hop. A registry extract names the immediate parent; that parent's filing may name a holding company in another jurisdiction; that one may name individuals or another entity again. Each hop is a fresh lookup against a different source, and you do not know how deep it goes until you stop finding new owners. Along the way anything that looks like a match against a watchlist has to be set aside with the document that raised it. Compliance wants the whole working file at the end — every entity reached, every source consulted, every discounted match and the reason — because the regulator asks for it.

Small-grant applications arrive with one or two attachments — usually a budget sheet, sometimes a letter of support. Before a panel member spends an hour on one, we want an agent to look at what came in and say whether there is enough there to assess, recommending proceed, return to the applicant, or hand to a person. The panel still decides.

Enhanced due diligence on a single institutional client currently takes an analyst around thirty hours and we run about a thousand a year. The analyst works through a defined bundle — corporate registry filings, adverse media, prior reviews, transaction narratives — and produces one written assessment where every statement has to be traceable to the document behind it, including where two sources disagree. Turnaround matters less than the assessment holding up when it is challenged.

Our operations teams keep asking the same kinds of questions about internal standard operating procedures — which approval a given transaction needs, what the cut-off is, which form applies. The SOP library is maintained centrally and reused by everyone; a typical question is settled by one procedure. Live transaction status comes from the operational system, not from the SOPs.

Supplier invoices from around two thousand suppliers across five countries arrive in widely varying formats, and we need the same thirty-odd fields off every one of them to post into the finance system. Low-confidence fields have to go to a validation step before anything posts, and a wrong value that gets through becomes a payment error, so per-field accuracy and the correction workflow are both hard requirements.

About a hundred thousand trade-deduction claims a year land as rows in a table, each carrying a short free-text reason a customer's clerk typed — shorthand, abbreviations, sometimes just a promotion name. We want a normalised reason code on every row, from a list we already maintain, so the claims can be matched against agreements later on.
